newsitem.title: USA: Wisconsin Gov. loses bond veto legal battle.
newsitem.headline: Wisconsin Gov. loses bond veto legal battle.

text.p: CHICAGO, Feb 3 (Reuter) The Wisconsin Supreme Court has trimmed Gov. Tommy Thompson's expansive veto powers by ruling that he cannot veto bond authorization amounts.
In a 4-to-3 decision released Friday, the high court affirmed that the governor can use his partial veto to shrink appropriation amounts, but cannot use that same power to revise bond authorization.

The court's decision was the first to rein in Wisconsin's unprecedented gubernatorial veto powers, according to State Sen Fred Risser, D-Madison, one of the state lawmakers who filed the lawsuit in January 1996.
A spokesman for Thompson and the attorneys handling the case for the governor's office were not immediately available for comment.
The lawmakers had charged that Thompson overstepped his constitutional partial veto powers when he decreased the amount of bonding authority in a transportation bill by $40 million.
While lawmakers had approved $172.8 million of bonds in the 1996-97 transportation bill, Thompson in December 1995 crossed that amount out, replacing it with $132.8 million of authorization.
Risser said while several cases had been filed in the past challenging Wisconsin gubernatorial veto power, the most expansive in the nation, the subsequent rulings ended up expanding that power.
This time, Risser said, the court drew the line between changing appropriations and changing bond authorization.

The court said that "in order for the write-in veto to apply, the bill at issue must be an appropriation bill" that sets aside public revenue for a public purpose or specified object. In this case, the court found "the sale of bonds is the commitment of the state to a debtor relation to those who purchase the bonds and is therefore distinguishable from an appropriation."
Still, Risser said he expects no real impact from the high court's ruling as Thompson chairs the state building commission, which ultimately decides on state bond issues.
"On the other hand it has a great psychological effect and it is a limit on this word 'partial,'" he said.
